baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Examines everyday gatekeeping and the contested remaking of immigrant citizenship in Cold War Canada.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Correction 2026-10-25: Basok/Bastable pp. 211–213 support the gatekeeping/citizenship claim. Immigrant cultural negotiation and resistance are independently supported by Iacovetta’s own 2019 article, pp. 29–30 and 35; the review’s resistance contrast on p. 217 is preserved and is not reversed. No full-book reading.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Places contradictory expectations about marriage, gender and family inside immigrant social-work encounters.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Correction 2026-10-25: Iacovetta’s own 2019 article, especially pp. 39–42, analyzes male-breadwinner/female-homemaker and egalitarian marital ideals, domestic-abuse counselling, female clients’ practical negotiations, and the limits of mediated case files. This replaces the earlier attribution to the joint review’s discussion of another author; it is a scoped article reading, not full-book verification.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: With Linda Kealey, Iacovetta answers Sangster’s Beyond Dichotomies, objecting that its polemic risks oversimplification and misrepresentation while welcoming debate (1996).
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: The opening expressly names Sangster’s essay and frames the response as disagreement among friends and colleagues. Linda Kealey is coauthor; she is not Gregory S.Kealey. Do not treat this as a single-author reply.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Replying to Iacovetta and Linda Kealey, Sangster welcomes their review but contests the simplification charge and treats gender as both standpoint and field (1996).
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: This is a qualified rejoinder: p. 247 stresses shared questions and theoretical overlap. It must not turn Iacovetta/Kealey into simple poststructuralist adversaries or erase the coauthor.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Citizenship programmes for newcomers and Indigenous peoples
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Bohaker and Iacovetta (abstract read) show that from 1950 to 1966 the Indian Affairs branch sat in the Department of Citizenship and Immigration and modelled its activities on citizenship campaigns for immigrants. A post-2000 comparison across the two fields. PhD context: 74 of 172 2009–2026 PhDs engaging Immigration, ethnicity & race in Canada also engage Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history (43%; lift 2.3), counted after removing shared anchors. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Canadian debates over gender as a category
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Pierson's 1991 essay opens on feminist historians' turn to deconstruction and discourse analysis, naming Scott's theory of gender as the most acclaimed example. Parr (1995) and the 1995–96 Left History exchange (Sangster; Iacovetta and Kealey; Dubinsky and Marks) argued over gender history and women's history; their citations are checked, and Sangster's own position is taken from her 2011 retrospect; the replies are read only as defences of gender history. PhD context: 64 of 328 PhDs engaging this group cite Scott (20% vs 9% of all; lift 2.12).

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Gender and class as simultaneous hierarchies, and gender history as a practice in Canadian women's history (1985–96)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period, her own words (Atlantis, 1985, read in full): women and children are not tied together as subjects by nature; 'What distinguishes feminine and preschooler from masculine and prime of life is not naturalness versus artificiality but proximity to power' (p. 39). She criticises the mid-1970s Canadian literature on reform for characterising 1880–1920 as 'an era of "maternal feminism"', seeing women's public actions 'definitionally as an extension of the private' (p. 41), and asks historians to 'stop shying away from the word "patriarchy"' and to 'allow as a possibility that gender/sex hierarchies and class hierarchies function simultaneously, each according to its own logic, often in conflict' (p. 44). She presents this as a change 'a good many others have already begun to suggest' (p. 39). The Gender of Breadwinners (1990), unread here, as reviewers quote it: Guildford (Atlantis, 1991, p. 140) says she rejects 'an ahistorical hierarchy of oppressions' (p. 8) and argues 'that class and gender are made and experienced simultaneously'; Bertaux (JEH, 1992, p. 241) quotes p. 9 on 'these galloping pairs—class/gender, male/female, market/nonmarket, public/private' whose meanings 'are multiple and mutable'. Reception in the Left History exchange (all read in full): Sangster calls the book 'One of the path breaking books on gender history' (1995, p. 120); Iacovetta and Kealey call her 'recognized as a leading practitioner of gender history' (1996, p. 222) and 'a major figure in the field', quoting her 1995 CHR essay (pp. 362–63) that 'gender history made masculinity and femininity commensurably problematical historically, while insisting that neither could be well understood without companion inquiries into the other hierarchies with which they were mutually intertwined' (p. 228); Dubinsky and Marks cite her for refraining 'from imposing one category - be it class or gender - on historical actors' (1996, p. 211). Criticism: Sangster (1996, p. 240 n. 2) characterises Parr's essay (its reprint in Gender and History in Canada, 1996, p. 11, unread here) as placing critics 'feminist and anti-feminist alike, in the same oppositional group' (Sangster's wording, not a quotation from Parr), notes that she had been reproached for not offering 'more criticism of historians such as Mariana Valverde and Joy Parr' (p. 240 n. 3), and, quoting Parr's line that the move to gender 'began from the post-structuralist premise that identities were made in relationships' (reprint p. 14), questions 'the prevailing assumption that gender history as the field, post-structuralism as the method, equals a superior, more broad-minded history' (pp. 244, 246). The 1995 essay itself is unread: its words here are quoted by Iacovetta and Kealey and by Sangster. Not a founding: the field's gender debate also runs through Pierson (1991) and Scott (edge_891). Later reading, labelled: a 2026 CHR 'great books' forum (abstract only) calls the book 'a path-breaking study that challenged established dichotomies in social theory'.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Her two-town study (1990) and 1995 essay deconstructed skill and treated 'portraits of experience' as 'interpretations, reclamations of sensations', while keeping 'materialist conceptions of work and the economy' (as read by Sangster, 2000)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Both Parr texts are unread (the existing Parr entry records the 1995 essay as known only through Iacovetta–Kealey and Sangster). Sangster 2000, read in full: the 'polar worlds of men's and women's work in small town Ontario' show 'the positive results of talking gender' (p. 151, citing The Gender of Breadwinners); Parr grouped with Tillotson, Mercedes Steedman and Creese as having 'deconstructed the notion of skill' while 'materialist conceptions of work and the economy are still in evidence, unlike the more radical, anti-materialist claims for deconstruction offered up by international scholars like Joan Scott' (p. 157); from the 1995 essay (p. 364) the sentence that portraits of experience 'were interpretations, reclamations of sensations which first had been organized, then claimed as experience' (p. 159, as quoted by Sangster). Moderate: a named reader's account.
